analogy.p: Imagine a village with one huge bakery that employs most of the villagers. When the bakery closes, the villagers have less money, so the café, newsagent and bus service lose customers and also close, and families leave. This is the negative multiplier effect. Regeneration is like opening a new factory or office that restarts the cycle. The analogy breaks down because a real economy is far larger and linked to the rest of the world, and workers cannot always take new jobs without new skills.
analogy.t: A town built around one big factory

bullets: **Primary**: raw materials taken from the land or sea, for example coal mining, North Sea oil and gas, farming, fishing, quarrying.
**Secondary**: processing and manufacturing, for example car assembly at Sunderland, steel making, shipbuilding, food processing and construction.
**Tertiary**: services that sell help or access rather than a physical product, for example NHS, retail, banking, tourism, education.

**Quaternary**: high-tech and knowledge industries, for example software, biotechnology, pharmaceutical research, IT consultancy and scientific research. Often counted inside the tertiary sector in official statistics.
The sectors are linked: a car factory (secondary) buys steel (secondary), uses mined iron ore (primary) and sells through dealerships (tertiary).
Developed countries (HICs) such as the UK usually have most jobs in the tertiary sector; low income countries (LICs) usually have most jobs in the primary sector.
The change in the balance of the sectors over time is called the **employment structure** of the economy, and it is shown on a triangular graph or a stacked bar graph.
core.h: The four sectors of the economy
core.p: An economy is split into sectors according to the type of work done. The **primary sector** extracts or harvests raw materials from the earth (farming, fishing, mining, quarrying, forestry). The **secondary sector** manufactures or builds things from those raw materials (making cars, steel, food, building houses). The **tertiary sector** provides services (shops, healthcare, teaching, banking, transport, tourism). The **quaternary sector** is knowledge based: research and development, information technology, consultancy and high-tech industries. The **UK economy** has moved steadily from the first two sectors towards the last two, and this change is the heart of this spec point.

bullets: Primary jobs fell sharply as coal mining collapsed (hundreds of thousands of miners in the 1950s to almost none today) and farming mechanised.
Secondary (manufacturing) jobs fell from around a third of jobs in the 1960s to under 10 per cent today, although output value is still large because factories are far more automated.
Tertiary jobs rose to around 80 per cent of all jobs; the biggest rises were in health, education, finance, retail, hospitality and business services.

**Exam skill**: when asked to describe a graph, quote data from the start and end (for example 'secondary jobs fell from 42 per cent to 15 per cent') and use words such as 'steadily', 'sharply', 'overtook'.
Manufacturing still matters: the UK is a major producer of aircraft parts, pharmaceuticals, cars and food, but these industries need fewer, more highly skilled workers.
A **triangular graph** has three axes (primary, secondary, tertiary) that add up to 100 per cent; a point moving towards the tertiary corner shows a more advanced economy.
Regional pattern: the loss of heavy industry hit the North East, Wales, Scotland, Yorkshire and the Midlands hardest, while the South East gained most service jobs.
core.h: How the UK employment structure has changed
core.p: In the early 1960s roughly half of all UK workers were in the primary and secondary sectors, with manufacturing alone employing around one in three people. By today services make up around four out of every five jobs and manufacturing is under one in ten. Primary jobs have fallen to only about 1 per cent of the workforce. The figures used in this note are rounded and illustrative, but the **direction and scale** of the change is what examiners want you to describe: a long, steady fall in primary and secondary employment and a large rise in tertiary and quaternary employment.

bullets: Traditional UK industries that declined: coal mining (South Wales, Yorkshire, Durham, Nottinghamshire), steel (Sheffield, Teesside, Port Talbot), shipbuilding (Clyde, Tyne, Wear, Belfast), textiles (Lancashire cotton, Yorkshire wool), car and engineering works (the Midlands).
Employment in manufacturing fell by millions between the 1960s and the 2020s.
The process is **uneven**: cities such as Sheffield, Glasgow and Newcastle experienced severe decline, while some areas of the South East grew rapidly.
Deindustrialisation is different from a recession: a recession is a temporary downturn, whereas deindustrialisation is a long-term structural change.
It is closely linked to **globalisation**, because production moved to countries with lower costs.
The area left behind often had many one-industry towns, so when the main employer closed there were few alternative jobs.
Deindustrialisation led to the creation of the **post-industrial economy**, in which services and knowledge industries dominate.
core.p: **Deindustrialisation** is the decline in importance of manufacturing and heavy industry (and of the primary industries that feed them) in an economy, measured by a fall in the number of jobs, the share of national output (GDP) or both. In the UK it began in the 1960s, accelerated rapidly in the late 1970s and 1980s, and continued as globalisation increased. It is not that the UK stopped making things; rather the **share of workers** and the **share of GDP** in industry fell, and many traditional industrial areas lost the industries that had defined them.

bullets: TNCs **offshore** production: they relocate factories abroad to cut costs, then import the finished goods back into the UK.
Newly industrialising countries (NICs) built their own heavy industry and could sell steel and ships more cheaply than the UK.
Containerisation and bigger ships made it cheap to ship goods around the world, removing the advantage of making products close to customers.
Fast global communications (internet, phones) let companies manage factories on the other side of the world.
Free trade agreements and the removal of tariffs reduced protection for UK industries.
Foreign-owned plants in the UK (for example car makers) can still close if the parent company shifts production elsewhere.
**Exam phrase**: 'cheaper labour costs overseas meant that goods could be produced and imported at a lower price, so UK factories lost orders and closed'.
core.h: Causes of deindustrialisation 1: globalisation and cheap labour
core.p: **Globalisation** is the growing connection of countries through trade, investment, transport and communication. Falling transport costs (container shipping, cheap air freight) and fast communication allowed **transnational corporations (TNCs)** to move manufacturing to countries where wages, land and regulation costs are much lower, such as China, India, Bangladesh and Vietnam. A UK factory worker earning a UK wage could not compete on price with a worker paid a fraction of that overseas, so goods that were once made in Britain (clothes, electronics, toys, steel, ships) were increasingly imported instead.

bullets: **Resource depletion**: the most accessible coal and iron ore deposits were used up, making mining more expensive than imports.
**Mechanisation and robotics**: a modern car plant makes more cars with far fewer workers than in the 1960s, so jobs fell even where output held up.
**Lack of investment and low productivity**: old factories and out-of-date methods meant higher costs and lower quality than competitors.
**Changing demand**: demand for ships, heavy machinery and cheap textiles fell; demand for finance, leisure and healthcare rose.
**Strong pound** at times made UK exports more expensive and imports cheaper.
**Environmental concerns**: the move away from coal towards cleaner energy (gas, renewables) reduced demand for coal.
**Exam tip**: separate causes into global (offshoring), local (resource ran out) and national (government policy) factors to build a structured answer.
core.h: Causes of deindustrialisation 2: resources, technology and demand
core.p: Several other causes combined with globalisation. The **cheap or easily reached resources ran out**: UK coal seams were deep, thin and expensive to mine, so imported coal was cheaper. **Automation and new technology** meant machines and robots replaced workers, so the same output needed far fewer people. **Demand changed**: customers wanted different goods and more services, and consumers switched to imported or higher-quality products. Finally, investment in new machinery in old industries was often too low, so productivity lagged behind foreign competitors.

bullets: **Privatisation**: selling state-owned industries to private companies, which then cut costs and jobs to make a profit.
**Closure of unprofitable pits and works** meant whole communities lost their main employer quickly.
**Deregulation of finance** ('Big Bang' 1986) helped London become a global financial centre.
**Regional policy** was patchy: some money went to old industrial areas, but not enough to replace the lost jobs quickly.
**Free trade membership** (EU single market) allowed imports to flow into the UK freely.
Policy decisions are debated: supporters said industries had to modernise; critics said communities were abandoned without a plan.
core.p: Government decisions speeded up the change. In the 1980s the government of the time reduced support for loss-making state-owned industries, privatised many (steel, coal, shipbuilding, rail) and let uncompetitive pits and factories close, the best-known case being the large-scale closure of coal mines that followed the 1984 to 1985 miners' strike. The government also encouraged growth of finance and services in the City of London (for example by deregulating the financial markets in 1986, 'Big Bang'). Later governments promoted free trade, membership of the EU single market and investment in services, which supported the shift away from industry.

bullets: **Economic**: high unemployment, long-term unemployment, lower incomes, empty shops, falling house prices.
**Social**: out-migration of young adults, ageing population, poorer health, loss of community identity, poverty, higher crime.
**Environmental**: derelict land and **brownfield sites**, contaminated soil, abandoned buildings, though some areas gained more open space as industry left.
**Political**: feelings of being 'left behind' and anger at national government in former industrial areas.
Some people benefited: cleaner air in cities and less noise and pollution once heavy industry left.
The multiplier effect can work in reverse (**positive multiplier**) when new jobs arrive, which is why regeneration focuses on attracting a large new employer.
core.h: Consequences of decline: the negative multiplier effect
core.p: When a major employer closes the effects spread through the local economy in what is called the **negative multiplier effect** (a downward spiral). Workers lose income and spend less, so shops, cafes and suppliers lose customers and also cut jobs. Unemployment rises, the area becomes less attractive to new businesses, young people and skilled workers leave, and the local council collects less in taxes, so services decline. Derelict factories and spoil heaps scar the landscape and put off investors. Social problems such as poverty, poorer health and crime can increase, and this can last for decades unless the area is regenerated.

bullets: **Sheffield (Meadowhall)**: a former steelworks site was redeveloped into a large shopping centre with a tram and motorway link, creating thousands of service jobs.
**Salford Quays and MediaCityUK (Greater Manchester)**: the old docks were redeveloped, and the BBC and other media firms moved there (from 2011), creating jobs in the quaternary/creative sector.
**Newcastle-Gateshead**: the Quayside has the Sage Gateshead concert hall, the Baltic art gallery and the Millennium Bridge, which attract visitors.
**Cardiff Bay**: a former coal-exporting dock turned into a centre for government, media and leisure.
Funding can come from the government, the EU (in the past), lottery money and private investors.
Evaluating regeneration: it improves the environment and creates jobs, but new jobs can be lower paid, and benefits may not reach people who lost the old jobs.
**Exam tip**: use a named example with place names and one or two facts to show case-study knowledge.
core.p: Many former industrial areas have been **regenerated**, meaning they have been redeveloped to bring new jobs, people and investment. Typical methods include cleaning up contaminated brownfield land, building new business parks and retail centres, developing tourism and culture, improving transport links, and relocating organisations to the area. Regeneration is rarely complete; it often creates jobs that are different from those lost (lower paid or requiring new skills), so some local people still lose out.

bullets: **Finance and business services**: banking, insurance and legal services are concentrated in the City of London and Canary Wharf, and also in Edinburgh, Leeds and Manchester.
**Retail and leisure**: more disposable income and car ownership led to out-of-town shopping centres and leisure parks.
**Health and education**: ageing population and expansion of universities created jobs everywhere in the UK.
**Tourism**: heritage, culture and sport attract millions of visitors a year.
**Quaternary examples**: software and gaming companies, medical research, aerospace research (for example engine design) and pharmaceutical research.
**M4 corridor** (west of London to Bristol and South Wales) and **Silicon Fen** (around Cambridge) are well-known high-tech clusters.
Why the South East? Good motorway, rail and air links, access to London markets and Heathrow, skilled workers and universities and more investment.
core.h: The growth of the tertiary and quaternary sectors
core.p: As industry declined, the **tertiary sector** expanded to provide most of the UK's jobs and wealth. Higher incomes meant people spent more on services such as leisure, education and healthcare; business services (accountancy, law, advertising, insurance) grew as companies needed specialist help; and London grew as a global financial centre. The **quaternary sector** grew too: the UK has strong universities, a skilled workforce, and world-class research in sciences, so IT, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals thrive. These jobs are well paid but need high levels of education, so they are concentrated in places with universities and good transport such as Cambridge, Oxford, London and the M4 corridor.

bullets: **Science park** features: close to a university, research laboratories, high-tech firms (biotechnology, IT, pharmaceuticals), shared facilities and a skilled workforce. Example: **Cambridge Science Park** (founded 1970 by Trinity College), part of the Cambridge cluster known as Silicon Fen.
**Business park** features: modern offices and light industrial units, landscaped grounds, ample car parking, edge-of-city location near a ring road or motorway junction.

**Locational factors**: cheaper land; room to expand; good road links (motorways, A-roads); near an airport (for example Stansted from Cambridge); attractive environment; nearby skilled workforce and housing; links with universities and research.
**Advantages for firms**: lower costs than the city centre, sharing ideas (**clustering**), shared facilities and a prestigious address.
**Advantages for area**: jobs and a boost to the local economy through the **positive multiplier effect**.
**Disadvantages**: car dependency, traffic congestion, loss of green-belt or farmland, and few jobs for unskilled workers, who may live far away.
**Exam phrase**: 'clustering allows firms to share ideas, suppliers and skilled workers, which encourages innovation'.
core.p: A **science park** is a group of scientific and technical knowledge-based businesses on a site that is usually near a university, so that companies and researchers can share ideas and use the university's expertise. A **business park** is a site on the edge of a town with office buildings and light industrial units, planned with space, parking and landscaping. Both are attractive to firms because land on the edge of a city is cheaper and less congested than the centre, there is room to expand, and there is easy access to motorways and airports. Staff enjoy a pleasant landscaped working environment.

bullets: **Land**: quarries and mines scar the landscape; factories and car parks cover greenfield land; spoil heaps and derelict sites need clean-up.
**Air**: burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide (global warming) and sulphur dioxide (acid rain); vehicle exhausts produce nitrogen oxides and particulates.
**Water**: factory waste and run-off can pollute rivers and groundwater; heavy industries use large volumes of water.
**Noise and visual pollution**: machinery, lorries and large buildings.
**Habitats and biodiversity**: building on greenfield land and removing hedges, trees and wetlands reduces wildlife.

**Ways of reducing impacts**: building on brownfield land; landscaping with trees and ponds; solar panels and energy-efficient buildings; recycling water and waste; encouraging public transport, cycling and car sharing; strict pollution regulations; green roofs and drainage ponds (SuDS) to reduce flooding.

**Case-study approach**: for the specification, know one example of modern industrial development and how it tries to be environmentally sensitive (for example a science or business park with landscaping, lakes and wildlife areas, and good public transport).
Evaluate: sustainable design reduces damage, but development still uses land, increases traffic and may disturb wildlife.
core.h: Impacts of industry on the physical environment
core.p: All industrial activity affects the physical environment, from the extraction of raw materials to the factory, the transport of goods and the disposal of waste. In the past, heavy industry caused major air, water and land pollution, scarred landscapes and destroyed habitats. Modern developments try to reduce these effects and are increasingly designed to be **environmentally sustainable**, using strict regulations, cleaner technology and careful landscaping. However even modern business parks still use land and generate traffic, so the effects are reduced rather than removed.

bullets: Characteristics: service jobs dominate; skills and qualifications matter; many people work in offices or from home; technology drives change.
Trade: the UK has a **trade deficit in goods** (imports exceed exports) but a **trade surplus in services**.
Rise of remote and flexible working, supported by broadband and online platforms.
Creative industries (film, music, design, video games) are a growing strength.
Inequality: high-skilled jobs in the South East pay much more than many service jobs elsewhere (link to the **north-south divide**).
Environmental aspects: fewer smokestacks, but increased use of data centres, air travel and cars.
Link to other topics: globalisation, the UK in the wider world, the north-south divide and sustainable development.
core.p: A **post-industrial economy** is one in which manufacturing is no longer the main source of jobs and wealth and services and knowledge industries dominate. The UK is a post-industrial economy: it makes high-value goods (aerospace, pharmaceuticals, high-end cars) with fewer workers, buys many cheaper goods from overseas, and earns income from services such as finance, insurance, education, creative industries and tourism. This brings opportunities and new problems. Wealth is high but unevenly spread, jobs can be insecure (zero-hours contracts, self-employment), and places that lost industry may still lag behind.

bullets: **Positives**: higher average incomes, cleaner air in many cities, growth of new industries, restoration of derelict land, modern jobs for graduates.
**Negatives**: unemployment and poverty in former industrial areas, widening regional inequality, loss of skilled manual jobs, lower job security, reliance on imports.
**Winners and losers**: well-educated people in the South East gained; low-skilled workers in the North and Wales often lost.
**Short-term vs long-term**: job losses were immediate, regeneration slow; some areas are still recovering decades later.
**Conclusion models**: 'Overall the impacts have been mixed, but for communities that lost their main industry the negative effects have been more severe and longer lasting.'
Always link ideas using 'because', 'this led to', 'as a result'.
core.h: Evaluating the changes and answering exam questions
core.p: Examiners want you to weigh up positives and negatives and reach a judgement. Deindustrialisation brought hardship to communities that depended on one industry, yet the shift to services has made the UK richer overall, produced cleaner cities and provided many highly paid jobs. The impacts depend on place: London and the South East gained; older industrial regions often suffered long-term. In a 6-mark or 9-mark 'assess' or 'to what extent' question, use evidence, give both sides, and end with a conclusion.

exam: **Describe** (2 to 4 marks): state what the data shows with figures and trends, and use direction words (rose, fell, steeply). One mark per point plus data for development.
**Explain** (4 marks): use a chain 'point, because, so, therefore'. For causes of deindustrialisation give two developed reasons, for example offshoring then loss of jobs.
**Suggest** questions: apply knowledge to unfamiliar data; use evidence from the resource.
**Assess / to what extent** (6 or 9 marks): give advantages and disadvantages with named examples, balance them and finish with a clear judgement (AO3 marks).
Use **named examples**: Cambridge Science Park, MediaCityUK in Salford, Meadowhall in Sheffield, coalfields of South Wales or the Tyne shipyards.
For graph questions (stacked bar or triangular graph), read the axis carefully, quote start and end values and calculate change; percentage change = change ÷ original × 100.
For 'why do businesses locate on the edge of the city' use at least three factors: cheaper land, room to expand, good road links, pleasant environment, skilled workers.
Link to other parts of the course (globalisation, north-south divide, UK in the wider world) to develop an answer.
Use geographical terms: negative multiplier effect, brownfield, regeneration, post-industrial, quaternary, clustering.
SPaG marks (4 on Paper 2): check spelling of key terms such as 'deindustrialisation' and 'tertiary'.

mistakes.r: Manufacturing declined as a share of jobs and GDP, but the UK still produces high-value goods using fewer workers and machines.
Give a developed cause: 'cheaper labour overseas meant imports were cheaper, so UK factories lost orders and closed'.
mistakes.w: Writing 'jobs were lost' with no reason.

mistakes.r: A recession is a temporary downturn; deindustrialisation is a long-term structural decline in industry.
Secondary = making and building things; tertiary = providing services such as banking, retail and health.
mistakes.w: Mixing up secondary and tertiary sectors (calling banking secondary).

mistakes.r: Quote figures and give the change: 'secondary jobs fell from 42% to 15%', and use words like steeply.
They are on the edge of the city, where land is cheaper and access to motorways is easier.
mistakes.w: Saying business parks are in the city centre.

mistakes.r: They are linked to a university and focus on research and high-tech knowledge-based industries.
mistakes.w: Saying science parks are just offices.

mistakes.r: Give both sides (new jobs, cleaner air, higher incomes) and make a judgement for 'assess' questions.
Describe the chain: job losses, less spending, more closures, more unemployment (negative) or the reverse (positive).
mistakes.w: Saying the multiplier effect is 'more money'.

summary: The specification asks you to know how and why the UK economy has changed: the causes of deindustrialisation and the decline of primary and secondary industry, and the growth of the tertiary and quaternary sectors including science and business parks and their effects on the physical environment. It matters because it explains why some UK regions are wealthy and others struggle, and it supports questions on the north-south divide and globalisation.

terms.d: Jobs that extract raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, mining and quarrying.
Jobs that manufacture goods from raw materials or construct things, for example factories and building.
Jobs that provide a service, such as retail, health, education, banking and tourism.
Knowledge-based jobs involving research and development, information technology and high-tech industries.
The decline of manufacturing and heavy industry in an economy, shown by falling jobs and share of output.
An economy where services and knowledge industries provide most jobs and wealth, rather than manufacturing.
The increasing interconnection of countries through trade, investment, transport and communication.
A large company that operates in many countries, often with production sites in low-cost countries.
Moving production or services to another country to cut costs.
The downward spiral in which job losses reduce local spending, causing more job losses and decline.
The upward spiral in which new jobs bring spending and so create more jobs.
Land that was previously built on, often derelict or contaminated, available for redevelopment.
Land not previously built on, often farmland on the edge of a town.
Redevelopment of a run-down area to bring new jobs, investment and improved environment.
A group of knowledge-based businesses on a site linked to a university, sharing ideas and facilities.
A planned site, usually on the edge of a town, with offices and light industry in a landscaped setting.
The grouping of similar or linked firms in one area, allowing them to share ideas, workers and suppliers.
When the value of imports is greater than the value of exports.

worked.ans: 64 per cent decrease (1 mark for 4.5, 1 mark for 64%). Reason (1 mark): offshoring/competition from low-wage countries or automation.
worked.q: UK manufacturing employment fell from 7.0 million jobs in 1971 to 2.5 million today (illustrative figures). Calculate the percentage decrease and suggest one reason. (3 marks)
steps: Round to the nearest whole number: 64 per cent.
Reason: cheaper labour overseas meant goods could be imported at lower cost, so UK factories closed.

worked.ans: Business parks locate on the edge of cities because land is cheaper than in the centre, so firms can afford spacious buildings and room to expand. They also have good access to motorways and ring roads, so staff can commute easily and goods can be transported quickly. Pleasant landscaped surroundings also help attract skilled workers.
worked.q: Explain why business parks are often located on the edge of cities. (4 marks)
steps: Point 1: land is cheaper than in the city centre.
Develop: so firms can afford large buildings with room to expand.
Point 2: good access to motorways and ring roads.
Develop: so staff can commute and goods can be delivered quickly.
Optional point 3: landscaped, pleasant environment attracts skilled workers.

worked.ans: Deindustrialisation caused serious damage in places like the South Wales coalfield, where pit closures led to unemployment and the negative multiplier effect, so shops closed and young people left. However, the UK economy as a whole gained, with growth in finance, services and high-tech jobs, and regeneration such as MediaCityUK shows that areas can recover. Overall I agree to a large extent for the old industrial regions, as the harm was greater and lasted longer, but for the national economy effects were mixed.
worked.q: 'Deindustrialisation has had mostly negative effects on the UK.' To what extent do you agree? (6 marks)
steps: Negatives: job losses, negative multiplier effect, out-migration, derelict land in places such as the South Wales coalfield.
Positives: growth of tertiary and quaternary jobs, cleaner air, regeneration at MediaCityUK.
Balance: effects depend on place and time; South East gained, former industrial areas suffered most.
Judgement: for communities that lost industry the effects were mostly negative and long lasting.
